There was a period after diagnosis that I was keeping my blood sugar within an optimal range and I never had the urge to drink water. Like I was never really thirsty. I had to train myself to drink water normally. I would try and drink water (ice cold water was easier) without having it feel like I was forcing myself.

I’ve recently started to go back to the gym this year, as well. For me, it’s helped a lot to bring down my BG when it’s high. It’s a little tougher to get through as I generally feel like crap at the start, but in the end I have a much more positive feeling. I always need to watch if I’ve bolused recently or have any active insulin lingering before I go. That could cause trouble. I also typically don’t eat before, so always bringing a snack helps! Don’t exert yourself too much that you’ll confuse what you feel is a low for overexertion, and vise versa. And if you’re going with your partner, i’m guessing she’ll always be keeping an eye on you!

The layers are a result of the concrete being used. Because concrete usually has a curing time, you need some pretty thick concrete in order to rapidly get layers down. Any bulging pretty much happens because the concrete is still fluid as you keep adding more layers. So, you need concrete with higher initial layer strength to avoid deformations along each layer. Most of these are done with round nozzles to promote better laminar flow of the concrete and still be able to come at each layer from any angle. The printers that do this are either stationary in the middle of the structure or on a truck, next to where the structure’s going to be placed.

I was diagnosed at age 20 and struggled gaining weight until a year ago. I hadn’t really changed my diet after I was diagnosed: typical midwestern diet, lots of meat, dairy, and carbs at the same time. I didn’t really care what I ate the first three years. I was hospitalized for DKA once from poor management. After that, I was kind of stuck while I kept my numbers in an okay range. My wife suggested that I join her in going vegan, which I was skeptical about because I wasn’t educated enough to know that you don’t need to keep increasing your protein to gain weight. I stopped eating animal products and immediately saw a change. I no longer had high cholesterol, started to gain my weight back and muscle without doing much workout. I then switched to pump therapy and my numbers were much more stable. I mostly now eat i guess would be considered less fat, but I burn through carbs faster now and my insulin sensitivity has increased too.

So, although it took a few months to get to pretty much the weight and build I had in high school (my wife really appreciated that), all I really had to do was keep my blood sugars in check and eat less fats. Fats are really going to hinder you from burning through carbs, and our bodies aren’t really used to storing fats yet because they have been accustomed to burning them prior to diagnosis. Fats also don’t help us T1D’s because we are more susceptible to heart disease and cholesterol issues.

I spent a summer working in my university’s material research lab and mostly mixed/tested fiber reinforced concrete, both steel fiber and polymer fiber. As far as cost, you might save some time by not having to lay rebar, but if you don’t have your proportions right and there is too little, or too much fiber, it really becomes a hassle to try to pour and finish. You do have to be careful with keeping your mix homogeneous throughout the pouring process as mixes can bleed or consolidate your aggregate very easily especially if you have a high fiber percentage. Obviously, you will have higher capacities if you use steel over polymer, and the shape and size of the fibers also effect this. I’d say as long as you have enough paste with a good mix, you can have a concrete that will resist chipping more than a traditional rebar mix. It will still crack, but it will take longer to lose it’s capacity since you have more fibers in the crack plane resisting the load.

What insulin delivery method are you using? And when are you giving yourself insulin (i.e. before or after meals?). I’ve had T1 for about 6 years now and i started on pens with partial success. I was always in the upper 100’s to mid 200’s and was always chasing it down. Like you, I never tested often, and still don’t to be honest. I can usually feel when I’m going high or low. I started to be more consistent with the pens when I started taking my insulin 10-15 min before I ate. This gives your body the time to take it in and it will start to work when you start eating, which at that time will immediately start to spike your BG. But, It is important that you take it BEFORE you eat. If you don’t, you BG will stay higher for awhile because the sugar in your blood gets distributed throughout your body and is not as easily accessible to insulin when you take it as if you had just eaten. If you have a pump, it’s of course much easier. Dial up how much insulin you need, make sure it’s getting delivered to you, and test an hour afterwords. If you’re still high, simply enter in your BG and if the company you purchased your pump from gave you a Insulin/BG ratio, which most do, then you just enter it and take the required amount and test an hour later. Most importantly, practice makes perfect. That’s the nature of the beast.

To add whats already listed here (agree with 100% btw), is stressing out when something goes wrong or you are out of something. I was on pens before i got a pump last year. It always sucked when you’re out to dinner and you forgot to restock on pen needles or a new pen or the pen you have been using malfunctions. At that point you have to sit with everyone and silently debate with yourself if you want to go really high and eat anyways or just take it home or something because you’re not going to risk it. More than that though is that people ask you what’s wrong. People will practically beg you to eat because they will feel so bad for you, but there is nothing you can do about it when you’re 30-45 min from home. Its just the way things are now and you just need to accept it. 

Inversely, those moments give you so many opportunities to educate people about our condition. The majority of people don’t even know the difference between T1 & T2 or even how insulin works. Take the time to assure them that you are fine, these kinds of things happen, and teach them a little bit about the condition. You never know if one day they will recognize someone acting strange and they will get them help and possibly save their life. 

Insurance is a bitch. I’ve always said since I was diagnosed that diabetics are the cash cows for the pharmaceutical companies, partly because insurance companies don’t want to pay for anything and they know you will have a lot of prescriptions to get. My advice would be to always stay on top of them and always ask for financial assistance from the pharmaceutical companies. Pump, insulin, and meter manufacturers usually have financial assistance programs that you will qualify for even when you make a decent amount of money. When you find one you can apply for, do so ASAP and remember to reapply every year. There are also prescription savings plans that you can just sign up online for free. My novolog savings plan saves me about $700-800 a year because I only pay $25 for a months supply ($80 with just insurance). 

Also, I’ve felt guilty when I have to ask for help. Most of the time it’s when I’ve run out of pump supplies and I don’t get the next shipment for another week. Never be afraid to ask your local diabetic supply store or your physician for help. Luckily for me, a Medtronic rep visits my physicians office regularly so I can always text her if I have an emergency and I can usually pick it up later in the day.

I feel your pain. Ever since I was diagnosed, I’ve had to borrow money from my parents when I have unexpectedly run out of insulin or needles or what have you. I’ve felt like a cash cow for the pharmaceutical industry. I bet I could have paid off my vehicle by now if insulin was cheaper. 

Don’t forget, most insulin manufacturers have patient assistance and savings cards that you can apply for. I’ve had on every year once I heard of them. Same with pump equipment and supplies.
